paper_description: This paper focuses on determining and reducing the maximum time an application holds a shared resource (Resource Hold Time - RHT) on a multiprocessor platform using global static-priority scheduling and the Priority Inheritance Protocol (PIP). It extends previous work by considering applications allocated on clusters of processors and introduces a method to adjust resource boost levels to minimize RHTs without compromising schedulability, highlighting the existence of multiple Pareto-optimal solutions in this multiprocessor context.

formal_description.statement: Assuming that A k is schedulable under PIP, there is at least one setting for the boost level of any global resource (shared by A k ) that satisfies Condition 12 (∀ R q ∈ R G k , boost q ≥ ⌈R q ⌉) without making A k unschedulable.

variables.⌈R_q⌉: highest priority of any task that may request R_q
variables.R_G_k: set of global resources accessed by application A_k

assumptions: Application A_k is schedulable under PIP.
Condition 12: boost_q ≥ ⌈R_q⌉ for all global resources R_q in A_k.
formal_description.conclusion: There exists a valid boost level assignment for global resources that maintains the schedulability of application A_k.

informal_sketch.intuition: If an application is already schedulable, we can always set the boost level of a resource to its minimum required value (which is the highest priority of any task that might request it) and the application will remain schedulable. This minimum boost level satisfies the condition that the boost level is at least the highest requesting priority.
steps: Start with an application A_k that is known to be schedulable under PIP.
Consider any global resource R_q shared by A_k.
Set the boost level of R_q to its minimum possible value, which is ⌈R_q⌉ (the highest priority of any task that may request R_q).
This setting of boost_q = ⌈R_q⌉ ensures that the condition ∀ R_q ∈ R G k , boost q ≥ ⌈R_q⌉ is met.
Since the application was initially schedulable and this boost level assignment is a valid configuration for PIP (specifically I-PIP), the application A_k remains schedulable.
key_insights: The minimum boost level for a resource (⌈R_q⌉) is always a safe starting point for schedulability.
This lemma establishes the existence of a schedulable boost configuration, which is crucial for the subsequent RHT reduction algorithms.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is essentially a restatement of Lemma 1, emphasizing that if an application is schedulable, we can always find a boost level for its global resources that keeps it schedulable. The proof relies on the fact that setting the boost level to the highest priority of any task requesting the resource (⌈R_q⌉) is a valid configuration for I-PIP and, if the application was initially schedulable, it will remain so.
steps: The proof directly follows from the reasoning in Lemma 1.
It is assumed that application A_k is schedulable under PIP.
For any global resource R_q, setting its boost level boost_q to ⌈R_q⌉ satisfies the condition ∀ R_q ∈ R G k , boost q ≥ ⌈R_q⌉.
This specific boost level assignment (boost_q = ⌈R_q⌉) is a valid configuration for the Immediate Priority Inheritance Protocol (I-PIP).
Since A_k was schedulable with its original resource access protocol and this new configuration is a valid I-PIP setup, A_k remains schedulable.
informal_sketch.pseudocode: This theorem is a statement of existence and its proof is constructive, as described in the steps. No specific algorithm is presented here, but the proof points to setting boost_q = ⌈R_q⌉ as a valid strategy.

Provides a concrete minimum boost level (⌈R_q⌉) that guarantees schedulability.
